According to the book *LTE Tutorial: Principles and Implementation*: **The half-wave dipole antenna is the most fundamental structural unit of antennas, much like molecules in chemistry.** Therefore, to gain a comprehensive understanding of antennas in various forms and applications, one must start from their origin: the working principle of the half-wave dipole antenna.


This article collates and summarizes the foundational knowledge related to half-wave dipole antennas, serving as a basis for studying more complex antenna system technologies.


# **Structure and Radiation of Half-Wave Dipole Antennas**


Structurally, a half-wave dipole antenna is composed of a pair of $1/4$-wavelength conductors, with a total length of $1/2$ wavelength—hence the name half-wave dipole antenna. This wavelength, of course, refers to the wavelength of the electromagnetic waves transmitted and received by the antenna. Electromagnetic waves in different frequency bands have different frequencies and wavelengths, meaning the calculated antenna lengths vary accordingly. **An antenna can only achieve optimal performance when its length is consistent with the wavelength/frequency of the electromagnetic waves it transmits and receives.**


![image.png](/images/blog/半波对称振子天线基础及其天线增益-1.png)


The wavelength formula is: $\lambda = C/f$ (where $C$ is the speed of light, $f$ is the operating frequency, and $\lambda$ is the wavelength). In the same medium, the operating wavelength of an antenna varies with frequency. The higher the frequency, the shorter the wavelength, and the shorter the corresponding antenna. Assuming the speed of light $C$ is $3 \times 10^8 \, \text{m/s}$:

- The wavelength corresponding to a 2.4GHz electromagnetic wave is: $(3 \times 10^8 \, \text{m/s}) / (2.4\text{GHz}) = 12.5\text{cm}$. The corresponding $1/2$ half-wave length is $6.25\text{cm}$, making the antenna length for a single dipole $3.125\text{cm}$.

The figure below shows the horizontal and vertical radiation patterns of a half-wave dipole antenna. The radiation intensity of a half-wave dipole antenna is uniform in all directions in the horizontal plane, and its half-power beamwidth in the horizontal plane is 360 degrees, meaning it acts as an omnidirectional antenna horizontally. In the vertical plane, its half-power beamwidth is 78 degrees, with zero radiation along the axis of the dipole. The 3D radiation pattern resembles the shape of a donut.


![image.png](/images/blog/半波对称振子天线基础及其天线增益-2.png)


Regarding antenna gain, using the electromagnetic field of a spherical uniform radiator as a reference, the antenna gain of a half-wave dipole antenna is 2.15dBi. Its beamwidth is relatively large, resulting in lower gain. In practical applications, if one wants to increase the gain of a dipole antenna, multiple dipoles can be combined to form an antenna array.


_Of course, as the most basic antenna type, the half-wave dipole antenna is often used as the reference unit for another antenna gain unit, dBd, where $\text{dBi} = \text{dBd} + 2.15$. Therefore, when evaluating an antenna's gain, one can use either dBi (relative to a spherical uniform radiator) or dBd (relative to a half-wave dipole antenna), with a difference of 2.15 dB between the two._


# **How to Increase the Gain of a Dipole Antenna?**


As mentioned above, for a standard half-wave dipole antenna, its antenna gain relative to a spherical uniform radiator is only 2.15dBi. This antenna gain is relatively low for many applications. So, how can the gain of a half-wave dipole be increased? After all, only by increasing the antenna gain can the wireless signals transmitted by the antenna cover greater distances. The answer is to connect multiple half-wave dipole antennas in parallel to form an antenna array. As shown in the figure below, multiple sets of identical unit dipoles are connected in parallel to the same feed point to form an array.


![image.png](/images/blog/半波对称振子天线基础及其天线增益-3.png)
